blocks.text: During electrolysis the positive ions (cations) move to the cathode and gain electrons from it: Cu2+(aq) + 2e- giving Cu(s), and 2H+(aq) + 2e- giving H2(g). Gain of electrons is reduction, and it always occurs at the cathode. Metal atoms formed may be deposited as a layer on the cathode or form a molten layer in the cell; hydrogen gas bubbles off. The negative ions (anions) move to the anode and lose electrons to it: 2Cl-(aq) giving Cl2(g) + 2e-, and 4OH-(aq) giving O2(g) + 2H2O(l) + 4e-. Loss of electrons is oxidation, and it always occurs at the anode.

Electrolysis is therefore a redox reaction. When molten zinc chloride is electrolysed, the cathode reaction is Zn2+(l) + 2e- giving Zn(s) (reduction) and the anode reaction 2Cl-(l) giving Cl2(g) + 2e- (oxidation); the electron loss at the anode balances the electron gain at the cathode, and the overall reaction is ZnCl2(l) giving Zn(s) + Cl2(g).

blocks.caption: Electrode reactions
rows: Cu2+ + 2e- gives Cu; 2H+ + 2e- gives H2; Zn2+ + 2e- gives Zn

blocks.prompt: Molten copper(II) bromide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which ions are present, where does copper form, and what are the two half-equations (Quick Check 10.4)?
blocks.explanation: Cu2+ and Br- ions are present. Copper forms at the cathode, Cu2+ + 2e- giving Cu, and bromine at the anode, 2Br- giving Br2 + 2e-. Overall CuBr2(l) gives Cu(s) + Br2.

items: Cathode: cations gain electrons, reduction (Cu2+ to Cu, H+ to H2). Anode: anions lose electrons, oxidation (Cl- to Cl2, OH- to O2). Molten ZnCl2 gives Zn at the cathode and Cl2 at the anode; electrolysis is redox.
